prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The

outputs.L1:
The boss is sitting at the desk. The boss does not look at her. The boss is waiting for the black telephone to ring, and she, too, waits for a summons from the boss, while he awaits the files from her. Her blue dress hangs about her body like a reused file folder, her hands clenched tightly around the documents. The filing cabinet might devour her, might take her hand clean off; the boss himself might devour her. The boss wants her—but the boss wants money more, always just a little bit more. The boss forever seems to want the money a bit more. The boss does not hear.

Outside, taxis idle, waiting for all the women down on the street. Across the way, another boss prepares for bed, while yet another, in the apartment above him—apartment X—rotates a Q-tip in his ear before sex, despite the instructions printed on the box.

We took my father out of the paper. The living will, the letters with their little capes, will depart the paper. Who will care for my children in the years to come? Who will care for my father? The will shall care for no one. A mere piece of paper cannot care for anyone, and I cannot care for everyone.

On certain nights I wake in a panic, unable to tell whether I am dead or alive. This year I dye my hair, so that I will not have to die.
outputs.L2: At her desk sits the boss, who won't turn his gaze toward her; he awaits the ringing of the black phone, while she too anticipates his call. He expects her to bring the files. Wrapped around her figure, her blue dress resembles a folder that's been used before, and her fingers grip the files tightly. Perhaps the filing cabinet will devour her, will snatch her hand away; perhaps the boss will devour her too. He desires her, yet his hunger for money runs deeper—just slightly more, forever slightly more, the money always calling to him a touch stronger. He fails to notice the cabs idling in the road below, ready for every woman on the pavement. On the opposite side, one boss readies himself for sleep, while a floor higher, in apartment X, another twists a cotton swab inside his ear before intimacy, ignoring the warning printed on the packaging. We removed my father from the document—the living will—and the letters, wearing their tiny capes, will depart from the page. Who will look after my children in the years to come? Who will look after my father? The will safeguards no one; a sheet of paper is incapable of protecting anybody. I cannot be everyone's protector. Certain nights I jolt awake in terror, unsure whether I'm living or gone. This year I color my hair so that dying can be avoided.
outputs.L3:
# The Dehumanizing Machinery of Work

The boss and his assistant exist in a state of mutual waiting, each anticipating a signal—the telephone's ring or the exchange of files—that keeps them perpetually locked in workplace tension. Their relationship is defined not by genuine interaction but by suspended anticipation, a shared limbo in which both parties await the next interruption that will animate their otherwise static existence. This dynamic reveals a workplace where human beings are reduced to functionaries, present only to respond to external triggers rather than to connect with one another meaningfully.

Within this environment, desire itself becomes subordinate to material interest. The boss desires the woman, yet ultimately values money more, and this hierarchy of wants exposes an uncomfortable truth: greed consistently overrides human connection and personal longing. Even the most fundamental human impulses—attraction, intimacy, the wish to be close to another person—are eclipsed by the calculating pursuit of profit. What might have been a moment of authentic feeling is instead converted into just another transaction, weighed and found wanting against the cold logic of financial gain.

This erosion of humanity is reinforced through imagery that deliberately blurs the boundary between people and objects. The woman's dress resembles a file folder, and the filing cabinet seems poised to consume her entirely, suggesting how thoroughly work dehumanizes and devours the individual. She is no longer a person but an extension of the office apparatus, her body absorbed into the very machinery of bureaucracy. The metaphor is both vivid and disturbing: the workplace does not simply employ people; it swallows them, transforming living beings into interchangeable components of an administrative system.

From this unsettling foundation, the speaker turns inward to grapple with the impossibility of genuine caregiving. There is a dawning recognition that legal documents—wills, contracts, the official paperwork meant to signify responsibility—cannot actually protect or care for anyone. They cannot shelter children, safeguard aging parents, or provide real comfort to those we love. The bureaucratic instruments we rely upon to demonstrate care are revealed as hollow gestures, incapable of performing the very function they promise. This realization deepens the poem's critique, extending it beyond the office and into the most intimate spheres of human obligation.

Ultimately, the poem culminates in an existential crisis in which the speaker confronts mortality directly. Unable to distinguish life from death, the speaker clings to superficial acts—dyeing one's hair, for instance—as symbolic attempts to ward off dying. These small rituals of maintenance and appearance become desperate defenses against the inevitable, futile gestures that expose our vulnerability in the face of death. In this final movement, the dehumanization traced throughout the poem reaches its logical endpoint: a self so estranged from vitality that it can no longer tell whether it is truly living, reduced to cosmetic rituals in a doomed effort to hold mortality at bay.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness piece that uses repetition of words like "boss," "waiting," "paper," and "take care of," and ends with a pun on "dye/die."
counterfactuals.output:
**Waiting**

The boss said wait, so I'm waiting, waiting by the water cooler where the paper cups stack up, paper thin, paper cups, and I'm waiting on the boss who said he'd take care of it, take care of everything, take care of me, the boss always says he'll take care of it but here I am waiting, paper in my hand, the paper he wanted, the paper I printed, waiting.

Boss, boss, where's the boss, the boss is in a meeting taking care of business, taking care of the paperwork, and I'm the paper pusher pushing paper while waiting, always waiting, the paper crumpling in my sweating palm, waiting for the boss to take care of the thing he swore he'd take care of.

Waiting rooms and waiting lists and waiting for the boss and the paper trail leads nowhere, paper cuts on every finger, paper airplanes I could fold instead of waiting, but no, waiting, the boss will take care of it, the boss takes care of everything, that's what a boss does, takes care, takes care, takes care until you're taken care of.

And the boss comes out, finally, no more waiting, and he's holding paper too, official paper, letterhead paper, and he says he's got to take care of the situation with the printing, the color's all wrong, the reds bled into the whites, and I say boss, I've been waiting, and he says son—

that's the last straw, that's the reason the whole batch is ruined, that's why I'll never work in printing again—

it's a shame you had to dye.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, associative prose poem about office life, power, desire, and death, blurring the line between the personal and the corporate.
counterfactuals.output:
# Quarterly Review

The elevator swallows me like a pill it isn't sure it wants to take. On floor twelve, my ambition waits in a beige folder, stamped *pending*. I have been pending for years. My name tag says I am *available*, and this is the great lie of the badge.

---

Consider the stapler: how it bites and bites and never eats. I loved someone in the copy room once, or I loved the warm hum of the machine and mistook it for a person. Their perfume was the smell of new toner. We made forty collated copies of a feeling and filed it under *miscellaneous*.

My manager keeps his heart in a locked drawer with the good pens. When he smiles, a spreadsheet opens somewhere and a cell turns red. He says *synergy* and three interns forget their mothers' faces. He says *let's circle back* and the calendar eats another Sunday.

---

There is a man in accounting who died in 1997 and no one told his inbox. It still fills. It fills like a grave fills with rain. His out-of-office reply is the most honest document in the building: *I am away. I am indefinitely away. I will respond upon return.*

We are all upon return.

---

I want the corner office the way a body wants more body. I want the window that owns a piece of the sky, a rectangle of weather I could call a subordinate. Power is just a chair that remembers the shape of the last person who wanted it this badly. I sit in it in my mind. It is warm. It is always someone else's warmth.

Desire, here, wears a lanyard. Desire schedules a meeting and does not invite you. Desire is the promotion given to a name that isn't yours, announced in an email that begins *Please join me in congratulating.*

---

At night the office keeps working without us. The fax machines dream. The plants photosynthesize the fluorescent moon. Somewhere the mainframe recites our resignation letters before we have written them, before we have found the courage or the exit.

The vending machine, oracle of the fourth floor, dispenses everything but mercy. I feed it my last coin. It gives me a bag of air and calls it *classic*.

---

When I go, let them not say I *passed*. Say the system logged me out. Say I was archived. Say my access was, at last, revoked, and the great glass doors—which never once loved me—hissed open like a mouth deciding I was finished, and released me into the parking lot, that gray field of exit, where the cars wait like the patient dead for someone, anyone, to turn the key and drive them home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of experimental fiction imitating the style of writers like Anne Carson or Claudia Rankine—fragmented, incantatory, about women, work, and family obligation.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inventory of a Woman Who Kept the House

*after the manner of accounting*

---

There is a word my grandmother used for the tiredness that lives in the wrists. I have lost it. This is the first entry.

---

Consider the dishcloth. Consider its wet and its gray. Consider the hand that wrings it, which is my hand, which was her hand, which will be—

no. I stop the sentence there. I do not consent to inheritance.

---

**On the subject of what is owed:**

My mother said *someday you will understand* and this was not a prophecy but a sentence, the kind handed down, the kind you serve.

Someday arrived. I understood. Understanding was not the reward they promised. Understanding was a second shift.

---

She calls at seven. She calls at nine. The phone is a rope. The phone is a rope and I am the bucket and the well is very deep and the water, when it comes, is her voice saying *are you eating.*

---

*The women in this family do not rest. The women in this family are load-bearing.*

I read once that a wall can hold a house up for a hundred years and no one thinks to thank the wall, no one paints the wall, the wall is simply the condition of the roof continuing to exist above the heads of the people who are not the wall.

---

**Question:** What is the difference between love and labor?

**Answer:** The difference is that no one asks the labor how it feels.

---

I made the soup. I made the soup because she is old now and her hands, the same hands, the wringing hands, have forgotten the soup.

The knife knew what to do. The knife remembered.

This is the cruelty: the body learns the work so well the work outlives the reason.

---

At the office I am efficient. At the office they say *she's a machine.* I want to tell them machines were built by someone. Machines had a maker who bent over them in the dark. Machines were also, once, only iron that did not yet know its purpose.

---

My daughter watches me at the sink.

I feel her watching the way you feel weather coming.

Turn around, I want to say. *Turn around and go outside and be a wall to nothing.*

But my mouth is full of the old word, the lost one, the tiredness that lives in the wrists, and I cannot warn her in a language I refuse to speak.

---

**Inventory, continued:**

One dishcloth.
One phone, ringing.
One knife that remembers.
One daughter, watching.
One word, missing.

The word was *soft.* The word meant a softness earned through use. My grandmother used it for the tiredness and also for the leather of an old glove and also, once, for me, when I was small and had not yet been put to work.

---

I set down the cloth.

I am trying to set down the cloth.

The cloth is still in my hand. I am telling you it is on the counter but it is in my hand and this is what I mean when I say inheritance:

the report of the action

and the action

do not match.

---

Turn around, daughter.

I am wringing something out.

It may be water. It may be the whole gray century of us.

Go outside. The soup can wait. The phone can ring into the deep well of the house we built with our backs.

Go.

I will be here.

I am always, it seems,

here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem exploring female anxiety and caretaking that moves from a workplace scene into meditations on a father's living will, children, and fear of death.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Body Holds

At the desk by 9 a.m., I answer
what the phones demand—yes, no,
I'll check, let me find someone
who knows. My smile is audible.
The coffee cools. A woman's voice
across the partition apologizes
for something that was never hers.

We are trained early in the grammar
of accommodation, the way *sorry*
becomes a hinge on which whole days
swing open. I forward the email.
I remember the birthday, the deadline,
the allergy, the thing he said he'd do
and didn't. My inbox is a nursery
of other people's needs, all crying
at once, and me with only two hands.

*

My father signed the papers in spring.
*Do not,* they say, *resuscitate.*
*Do not keep breathing what cannot breathe.*
He handed me the folder like a lunch,
casual, as if I would not carry it
into every room I enter now.

I am the one who will decide.
The daughter always is. My brothers
will be *consulted*—a softer verb,
a chair pulled back from the table.
But the pen, when it comes,
will find my fingers already curled
around the shape of letting go.

*

My children do not know yet
that love is mostly logistics—
the packed bag, the wiped counter,
the fever measured at 3 a.m.
while the house sleeps its innocent sleep.
They think I am simply *there,*
the way the ceiling is there,
the way water is.

I want to teach them to worry less
than I do. I want to hand them
a lighter folder. But I feel it
threading through them already,
the girl especially, how she asks
if I am *okay,* how she watches
my face for weather.

*

And underneath it all, the fear
I fold into the smallest drawer:
that one day I will be the one
in the bed, the living will,
the daughter's hand deciding.
That the phones will ring
in a room I have left,
and someone will say
*let me find someone who knows,*
and no one will.

*

Tonight I stand at the sink
and let the water run too hot.
The house exhales around me.
Somewhere my father breathes
his numbered breaths. Somewhere
my daughter dreams she is a bird.

I hold the plate until it's clean.
I hold it longer than it needs.
This is the prayer I know:
to keep my hands full,
to keep them moving,
to keep them from the truth
that holding on and letting go
are the same verb,
learned young,
practiced daily,
never mastered.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
